case: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
facts: His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru, head of Edneer Mutt in Kerala, challenged the Kerala Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1969 under Article 26 regarding the right to manage religiously owned property. During pendency, Parliament passed the 24th, 25th, and 29th Constitutional Amendments.
issues: What is the extent of Parliament's amending power under Article 368?
Can Parliament amend or take away Fundamental Rights?
Are there inherent limitations on the amending power of Parliament?
decision: By a 7:6 majority, the Supreme Court held that while Parliament has wide powers to amend any provision of the Constitution including Fundamental Rights under Article 368, it cannot alter or damage the 'Basic Structure' or essential features of the Constitution.
ratioDecidendi: The power to amend under Article 368 is not the power to abrogate or rewrite the Constitution. Basic features such as democracy, secularism, rule of law, separation of powers, and judicial review cannot be destroyed.
quotations: Article 368 does not enable Parliament to alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution.

case: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
facts: Maneka Gandhi's passport was impounded by the Regional Passport Officer under Section 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act, 1967 'in the public interest'. When she requested reasons for the impounding, the Government refused to furnish them stating it was not in the interest of the general public.
issues: Is the right to travel abroad part of personal liberty under Article 21?
Does 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 require the procedure to be fair, just, and reasonable?
decision: The Supreme Court expanded Article 21 dramatically, holding that the 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 must be fair, just, and reasonable, and not arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive. Introduced the principle of procedural due process.
ratioDecidendi: Articles 14, 19, and 21 are not mutually exclusive but form a golden triangle of constitutional protection. Any law depriving personal liberty must satisfy the test of fairness and reasonableness under Articles 14 and 19.
quotations: The procedure prescribed by law for depriving a person of his life or personal liberty must be right, just and fair and not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive.

case: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017)
facts: A 9-judge Constitution Bench was constituted to determine whether the Right to Privacy is a fundamental right under the Indian Constitution, following challenges to the Aadhaar scheme.
issues: Is there a fundamental right to privacy under the Constitution of India?
Does privacy emanate from Article 21 and Part III?
decision: Unanimously held that the Right to Privacy is a fundamental right protected under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution. Overruled previous judgments in M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) to the extent they held privacy was not a fundamental right.
ratioDecidendi: Privacy is an intrinsic part of life, personal liberty, bodily autonomy, and informational self-determination. Any state infringement on privacy must satisfy the three-fold test of legality, legitimate state aim, and proportionality.
quotations: Privacy is the ultimate guarantee of freedom, dignity, and autonomy.

case: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018)
facts: A writ petition was filed by dancer Navtej Singh Johar and others challenging Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, which criminalized 'unnatural offences'.
issues: Is Section 377 IPC unconstitutional to the extent it criminalizes consensual adult samesex relations?
decision: The Supreme Court unanimously read down Section 377 IPC, holding that consensual adult sexual acts of whatever orientation do not constitute an offence. Overruled Suresh Kumar Koushal (2014).
ratioDecidendi: Constitutional morality triumphs over social morality. Sexual orientation is an inherent facet of human dignity, personal liberty, and privacy under Article 21, and discrimination based on sexual orientation violates Article 15.
quotations: History owes an apology to the members of this community and their families for the delay in providing redressal.

case: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017)
facts: Shayara Bano challenged the practice of Talaq-e-Biddat (instant triple talaq) by which a Muslim husband could divorce his wife instantaneously by pronouncing talaq three times.
issues: Is the practice of Talaq-e-Biddat protected under Article 25 (Freedom of Religion)?
Does instant triple talaq violate Article 14 (Equality)?
decision: By a 3:2 majority, the Supreme Court declared the practice of Talaq-e-Biddat (instant triple talaq) unconstitutional, illegal, and void.
ratioDecidendi: Instant triple talaq is manifestly arbitrary and lacks legal efficacy. What is held to be bad in theology cannot be good in law.
quotations: Talaq-e-biddat is manifestly arbitrary in the sense that the marital tie can be broken capriciously and whimsically.

case: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
facts: S.R. Bommai, Chief Minister of Karnataka, challenged the dismissal of his government and imposition of President's Rule under Article 356 following floor test disputes.
issues: Is the proclamation of President's Rule under Article 356 subject to judicial review?
What constitutes breakdown of constitutional machinery?
decision: Held that the power under Article 356 is a conditional power and the proclamation of President's Rule is subject to judicial review. Declared Secularism and Federalism as basic features of the Constitution.
ratioDecidendi: The floor of the Legislative Assembly is the only place to test the majority of a government, not the Governor's subjective satisfaction.
quotations: Secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution. Federalism in the Indian Constitution is not a matter of administrative convenience but a principle of constitutional governance.

facts: During the National Emergency declared in 1975, the President issued an order under Article 359(1) suspending the right to move any court for enforcement of Article 21.
issues: Can a writ of Habeas Corpus be filed under Article 226 during National Emergency when Article 21 is suspended?
decision: By a 4:1 majority (Justice H.R. Khanna dissenting), the court held that no person had any locus standi to move any writ petition for Habeas Corpus challenging illegal detention during Emergency. Justice Khanna's dissent became legendary.
ratioDecidendi: Overruled later by 44th Amendment and Puttaswamy judgment. Justice Khanna wrote: 'Rule of law is the antithesis of arbitrariness... Life and personal liberty are not creations of the Constitution.'
quotations: State has no power to deprive a person of his life or personal liberty without the authority of law. (Justice H.R. Khanna Dissent)

facts: Bhanwari Devi, a social worker in Rajasthan, was gang-raped for attempting to stop child marriage. Women's rights groups filed a PIL for protection against sexual harassment at the workplace.
issues: Are there effective enforcement mechanisms for fundamental rights of working women against sexual harassment at workplace?
decision: The Supreme Court formulated the historic 'Vishaka Guidelines' for the prevention of sexual harassment at workplace under Articles 14, 19, and 21, drawing upon CEDAW international convention, binding until statutory law was enacted.
ratioDecidendi: Gender equality includes protection from sexual harassment and right to work with dignity, which is a universally recognized human right.
quotations: Sexual harassment at workplace is a clear violation of the fundamental rights of gender equality and right to life and liberty.
